INTRODUCTION:
Liver cancer is the third leading cause of cancer mortality globally, with HCC comprising 80% of cases. Glycosylation abnormalities are linked to tumor invasion and metastasis, with elevated fucosylation, sialylation, and branched glycans observed in HCC tissues and serum. Previous studies identified glycosylated proteins like AFP and DCP as HCC biomarkers, but glycan verification remains challenging due to lack of biological templates. Lectin microarrays enable rapid glycan profiling by recognizing specific glycan motifs. This study aims to analyze pre- and post-operative serum glycan changes using lectin microarrays to evaluate their association with HCC progression and prognostic value.

MATERIALS AND METHODS:
The study enrolled 65 HCC patients (57 men, 8 women; mean age 57.05±10.66 years) and 20 healthy controls. Serum samples were collected pre- and post-surgery, with exclusion criteria including other liver diseases and chemotherapy. Clinical characteristics were assessed using CTP, TNM, and BCLC staging. Fifteen lectins (AAL, LTL, etc.) were used to recognize specific glycan structures. Serum glycoproteins were depleted, labeled with Cy3, and analyzed via lectin microarrays. Statistical methods included Mann-Whitney tests, ROC analysis, and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis.

2. 19 free-glycans were identified in CSF, in addition to 64 N- and 13 O-glycans
3. Two specific free-glycans (Hex₁ and HexNAc₁Hex₁Neu5Ac₁) showed significant differences between AD patients and controls
4. These two free-glycans had good ROC curve performance (AUC > 0.8), suggesting biomarker potential
5. The study found that AD patients had significantly less intact N- and O-glycans and more asialylated fragments than healthy controls
6. Sialylated biantennary and bisecting biantennary N-glycans were higher in patients with AD than in healthy controls
7. O-glycan sialylation was decreased in patients with AD compared to disease control patients and healthy controls

The paper suggests that these glycosylation changes may be related to the pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease, particularly in relation to amyloid-beta production and tau protein glycosylation.

The authors acknowledge that further validation is needed through larger multi-center studies, and they suggest considering other factors like gender, comorbidities, lifestyle, and genetics in future research.
